(This review is quite long, but you can just read the first sentence of the numbered topics if you prefer, since the rest is purely my view of the mentioned aspects. I think this game isn't fully enjoyable if you just rush the reading, which is one of the points that I mention here!)

How to enjoy this game:

1 - Ignore the reviews when people complain about the combat. It's different, clunky and not easy to grasp- you'll get used to it after your second hour or whatever, so just ignore them. They work for Salamandra. They want to prevent Geralt from recovering Kaer Mohren`s stolen secrets and contribute to the hostility towards nonhumans (they also hate Leo).

2 - Don't skip dialogues. I strongly advise against follow that massive, almost unbearable impulse (we all have felt that) of clicking during dialogues to skip them, even when you've already read the subtitles; the whole thing becomes much more immersive if you just listen to the voice actors and allow the dialogue to play at its own rhythm. 

3 - Be prepared to read a lot! You really shouldn't underestimate the Journal entries: the ones about Characters, Locations and Monsters, and the Glossary, they all have lots of useful data, little bits of information that are more than just flavor text; they add comprehension, life and detail to the whole game, making it such a rich and planned environment. Well, I admit that maybe I got a little overhyped here, but it's just because I really really liked the world of the game! 

4 - Research, explore, kill things. Certain side quests cannot be completed after advancing through the main story, so... what are you waiting for? Yes, you have a main quest to complete, but don't you think that the monster contract about killing some human-eating specter dogs is a little more urgent? The main quest is there and has to be completed; it's not going anywhere. But if you complete a chapter and move to a new area, you can't go back to the previous one to help that guard with his ghoul problem, so explore everything;

5 - Gather ALL the herbs! (Ginatz Acid, Albar's Crystals and White Vinegar are the best ones to sell in the beginning, so stock them up!) And organize your alchemy bag. You'll notice that the bag has six rows, which is the same number of primary components. It will be much useful if you use one row to each one (I like to use the order that appears in the bag: Vitriol, Rebis, Aether, Quebrith, Hydragenum, Vermillion). Also there are three secondary ingredients, which can improve the effects of potions - I like to order them as Albedo, Nigredo and Rubedo. Special ingredients can go to the last line (you're not going to find much Vermillion in the beginning anyway). The alchemy system is interesting, and keeping your inventory tidy not only makes things easier, but gives a good feeling on it. But don't exaggerate - I personally don't like having 30 of four different ingredients that gives Vitriol and Albedo, there is no need for it. You can keep one type of each primary/secondary ingredient and sell the rest. Don't let your inventory be a mess!

6 - Play it on hard. I'm serious here. First of all, there are monsters everywhere, horrible beasts and creatures that terrorize the common people and prevents them from sleeping; it came to the point where people started to perform sinister rituals and experiments on children, mutating their bodies to the extreme and giving them superhuman endurance, senses and reflexes, so they can undergo extreme training in order to grow up and become the infamous Witchers, skilled monster hunters the that people despise, and yet they need them. Why would they have to do all of that if Geralt of Rivia (our most famous Witcher) was able to kill the creatures with a single swing of his sword? No. The monsters are not to be taken lightly, even for a Witcher, even for THE Witcher. If the combat becomes too easy, you may think "hell, THESE are the horrible creatures that make people scared at night? And they are giving me 500 orens to do something their farmers could do? Seriously?"

"Hard" is a difficult that can be beaten by anyone - "Medium" and "Easy" is simply unfair. Many people complain that the game is actually easy in the end, even on HARD. So...

7 - You can use Aard and Igni signs, of course, but don't SOLELY depend on them. The five Signs (think about them as "small, quick spells") are very useful, but these two (knockback and fire, respectively) are way too overpowered if you decide to max them right from the beginning. Remember, you have two swords, you're a WITCHER - the signs are secondary tricks. Burning everything with Igni is nice, but what's the fun in letting that meteorite sword resting by your back and letting magic do the job? 

8 - Don't Load Game because you regretted a choice. Think seriously before making your decicions, accept the consequences of your actions. Imagine how Geralt (and here I mean YOUR vision of Geralt) would act, what he would not do, and if he could do that thing depending on the circunstamces; there are going to be dilemmas and hard choices. Sometimes, and more often than Geralt would like, it will about choosing the lesser evil.

9 - Prepare your potions. I like having at least 3 Swallow (my favorite potion so far, a real lifesaver) strenghtened with Rubedo (the Additional Ingredients page of the Glossary will introduce you to one of favorite small aspects of this game) Think about the witcher's preparations to combat, and how they have their equipments ready before fighting monsters; the potions are part of them, try to keep some of your favorite potions, oils and bombs ready when you need it!

There are some downsides observed by many people; the Inventory system is one, and the infamous swamp is another, and of course we cannot forget these two suspects from chapter two that demand more than some CSI episodes for you to fully investigate them. But try to think about those flaws as part of the game. They are not game-breaking, and if you just keep playing it, you learn they're not as big as an issue. If you really can't bear some of the downsides, there are always mods that can solve some issues without breaking the experience. 

And, of course, remember that The Witcher 2 comes after this, and then The Witcher 3. There is a mechanic that allows you to import your save from TW1 to TW2, and the save from TW2 to TW3. Think that all the choices you've made today are going to follow you in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt!

(10 - If a woman in a witch's hut tells you she's selling an oil, buy it! You gonna need it)

The first entry of the Witcher series is still among my favorite RPGs out there and if you ask me it can still stand the test of time.

The Story follows Geralt of Riva, a Witcher - a mutant and monsterslayer hired for gold, having lost his memory.
While trying to regain it, the residence of the witchers is attacked by an unknown group, which is trying to steal the secret mutagenic substances and formulas from the witchers, which they guarded closely ever since.
After the attack, Geralt then goes on his way to uncover who was behind this attack, what this group wants with their secrets and is going after their leader.

Of course, the graphics aren't on par with some newer titles and are a bit dated, though it still has a lot of attention to detail and creates a great atmosphere.
When it comes to atmosphere, the soundtrack has to be mentioned as well, as it's not just complimenting the game in a great way, it's fantastic on it's own.

Most parts of the game are pretty much working as any other 3rd person RPG (you can play it also in a kind of isometric perspective, clicking on the ground to move Geralt, though i've never played it that way, as it felt weird) as you walk and run around, looking over Geralt's shoulder, talking to people with different answering options, going on sidequests etc.

The combat however is a bit different than what you might be used to. You don't have to click away the whole time to attack, it's more of a click-combo-system where you click, then Geralt is in an attack animation and near it's end the mouse cursor changes, indicating that you can click now to create a combo chain.
It takes a bit getting used to it, but once you figured it out, it works rather good.

You also have to decide weather to use a silver or a steel sword, depending if your opponent is a monster or a human.
Still to easy for you? Well you also have three different fighting styles per each sword type: the strong-, fast- and group-style.
So each enemy has to be countered by it's own weakness, which gives the combat in the game a bit of a "rock, paper, scissor"-feeling, which works quite well, but together with the rather clumsy way of how the combat plays out, it can get a bit tedious at times.

Where the game really shines in my opinion, is the story, the characters and the overall atmosphere. 
As already mentioned, the music does it's fair share of drawing you into this world, while Geralt and the other characters do the rest. They're interesting, sarcastic, snarky, evil-tongued and just very compelling overall.
It's a rather dark world, filled with racial prejudice towards Nonhumans like elves and dwarfs, cursing and swearing and a lot of violence.
Getting to know the involved parties, you also realize that not everything is as black and white as you might think, which is especially hard when it comes to the many decisions you have to make.

Do you want to side with the nonhumans, or the order of the flame rose? None of them are saints, none of them are necessarily evil monsters.
Do you side with the town witch, which is accused of tampering with the town folk with no real evidence or do you protect her from the mob, not being able to shake the feeling, that she is indeed involved in something devious?
There is not always a "right" choice and even if you think you did the right thing, you might find out, that your choice led to something even worse.

So, if you're interested in a gritty fantasy RPG, i'd recommend you have a look at the Witcher.
If you can overlook the dated graphics and the rather clumsy combat, you might find yourself a true gem here.

This is an interesting one. First Witcher I played was The Wild Hunt aka the 3rd one. Which means I kinda got spoiled by experiencing the newest and greatest the Witcher series (thus far) has to offer. So there might be some comparisons to that one so keep that in mind.
Anyway lemme first cover the things that I like about the Witcher.
+ The number one thing that kept me in the game is the story. It's surprisingly engaging and kept me playing despite the games flaws which I will get to. It has some twist and turns which the final one I kinda predicted but it was still enjoyable. Overall amazing main story. There are also several side stories that are interesting aswell. 
Next positive is the way you can effect the story. Often you can effect how the games different stories turn out or you try to effect it the way you want. This means you get different endings to your side stories and of course the main one which I really want to experience second time to get a different ending. And I just wanna say that I'm so impressed that they managed to do this in 2008. Hats off to you. I also like the fact that this isn't a happy go lucky fairytale and that it has darkness and tragedy in it. This is also prominent in the choices that you are present with, everything isn't good or bad, black or white and I appreciate that.
 Another positive I'd say is the "complexity" of the combat, and by "complexity" I mean compared to other Witcher games. You have steel sword which is meant against humans and wolves bears etc, typical stuff that you would find in a Finnish forest. Or I guess in this case, Polish forest. Silver sword is another weapon in your arsenal which is for everything else aka for monsters. Game offers 3 different fighting styles, fast, strong and group. Fast is most effective against smaller enemies, since they can dodge the strong ones. Strong is great against big enemies, since it deals a lotta damage, as Phil Swift would put it. Group deals damage to everyone around you at a reduced cost of damage. You're also able to execute combos by precisely tapping the attack key when you are supposed to. So some might ask "why shouldn't I just spam the attack key, that seems a lot easier". Sure try it, let's how far that gets you.
I'd say that's it for the positives and now for the not so great stuff.
- I know this is kinda obvious and a cheap shot against the game but graphics are just really dated. The environment, the buildings, character models... jeez.
 Next negative would be "open-world" aspect of the game, which well it isn't. It's more like ok sized areas connected with loading screens. Also, every single building has a loading screen, nice.
 Another negative would be the overall clunkiness of the game, in the movement and the combat especially. Even though I enjoy the combat somewhat, it's hindered by the amount of CLUNK. It feels like Geralt is wearing 100% cotton selvedged denim onesie.
 Also the minigames suck. Fistfighting, nah. Drinking, nah (in the game of course you silly). Poker dice, meh. Only reason I played these is because I'm a completionist, which in this cased sucked.
 The last negative has to be the amount of crashes, dear god. This game must've crashed more then all of Bethesda games that I own combined. Later on I learned that this can apparently be prevented if you only keep 10 or less saves, otherwise the game turns in to Mustang and activates crowd mode.
So I played through the game once which took me 60 or so hours, some of which where spent retreading and in the main menu since the game crashed a bunch. And do I recommend it? Well there are couple of ifs and buts. If you have only played games that have released in the last 5 years (which in and of itself is a sin), then avoid this. Also if you hate or just can't stand older games you should also pass (but you can always take a risk). But to everyone else, this is a game with an amazing story that makes you wanna play again to see how things end up if I choose differently, despite its downfalls.
For myself I was just on the edge of not liking this game, but the story is just that great and won me over. I might even play this again to see where things end up if I pick different choices.

[h1]The Witcher: Enhanced Edition.[/h1]
[i]Something ends, something begins…[/i]

The Witcher: Enhanced Edition is a fantasy RPG, based on [i]The Witcher[/i] book series (1993-1999) by Andrzej Sapjowski. The game goes to great lengths to bring the world and thematic concepts of the books to life, and does so impeccably well, while also adding an original folk-fantasy flavor to the experience. TW:EE thoroughly invests the player with its meticulously crafted philosophical abstractions and emotionally involving character stories; the game’s faults paling in comparison to these strengths. But enough broad banter my fellow Witcher, let’s hit the path.

[i]You, are Geralt of Rivia - The Witcher.[/i] A Witcher is a genetically modified human, altered for the purpose of attaining superhuman abilities, which allow them to slay monsters that plague the human race. You’d think this would make Witchers revered as heroes amongst society, but their incredible physical attributes are ironically viewed as unnatural, making them social outcasts and a perceived necessary evil by most. In TW:EE, the mutagens which produce genetically altered Witchers have been stolen, by a secret organization known as Salamandra. It becomes your quest, as Geralt; to track down, expose, and destroy this conglomerate, as well as recover your Witcher’s secrets.

As stated before, The Witcher video games are continuations of [i]The Witcher[/i] novels, of which there are two anthologies of short stories, and five books in the main saga. They expand upon the world of The Witcher with infinite levels of depth, and reading them before you play will enhance your emotional connection to the events of the game ten-fold. TW:EE contains copious references to the books through its quotes, themes, and lore, and catching these call-backs is a real treat. CDPR handled the subject matter of the books with expert hands, and this game is a true sequel to the novels as a result of their hard work and care.

In terms of the look and sound of The Witcher: EE, I’d say it fares pretty well almost a decade later. The graphics were high-end for their time, and still have a certain art-based allure to them, however they don’t compare to anything released today. The environments are sweepingly beautiful and realistically structured, but the finer details; especially human faces, don’t hold up at all. On the other hand, the music is near-perfect. The soundtrack always fits where it’s presented, and the vibrant, exotic melodies are highly responsible for crafting the incredible atmosphere and folktale vibe that TW:EE is known for.

The world of The Witcher is designed to resemble a gritty, pastoral mid-European country, and is divided into distinct, free-roam levels that change each chapter. It’s not an open world game, but the places it gives you to explore are vast, and interconnected with other locations, interiors, and dungeons. The NPCs add a lot to the personality of the world too, as they’ll react to the circumstances of their environment, such as getting under structures when it rains. Its little things like this that help make the game world feel like a living, autonomous place. This brings to light a central tone of The Witcher: the convoluted complexity of life.

Much of what you do in TW:EE can be blanketly described as “questing”, and every quest is enjoyable in some way. There are monster contracts which immerse you in the role of Geralt as a Witcher, character/conflict quests which bring you closer to the intriguing personas found in the Kingdom of Temeria, and slow-burning main quests that lead you to your overall goal. Completing these quests earns you experience points used for perks in a slightly over-complicated leveling system, but the progression feels meaningful regardless, due to Geralt’s rising mastery of his skills.

Speaking of Geralt’s skills, combat is where he applies nearly all of them. The swordplay in The Witcher gets a lot of hate, and while to an extent it’s antiquated due to being a semi-turn based system, there’s still a ton of variety. As a Witcher you carry a silver sword for monsters and a steel one for humans, using strong, fast, or group fighting stances depending on your opponent(s). Witchers also have five magical “signs”, which are essentially simple combat spells. There’s an extremely in-depth and lore supported potion brewing system as well, which really authenticates the gameplay side of being Geralt. These elements come together cohesively, and function best at higher difficulties.

Though this somewhat undercuts everything I’ve said so far, I feel it’s important to mention that The Witcher’s game engine makes everything feel kind of wonky. Minor bugs run rampant, and there is a rare crash or frame drop every now and then. The physics system is weak and the facial animations are too, as well as the delivery of the dialogue by the voice actors on occasion. However, none of that could take away from the valid praise I’m about to sing about various narrative elements of TW.

One of the hold-overs from the books that found its way into the narrative of The Witcher: EE, are deep, philosophical and intellectual concepts. For example, Geralt often grapples with his identity as a Witcher. He believes his role is to fight evil (such as murderous monsters), but finds that as humanity progresses, evil has embedded itself within society through ideology, and impurely motivated; morally grey conflicts. Not only does this make him second guess his purpose, but also whether or not he should even get involved in human conflict; as taking a side in a morally grey situation can only mean choosing a lesser evil, which is still evil; [i]the antithesis[/i] of what Geralt seeks to propagate. It’s these types of complexities that make The Witcher so enthralling, and the narrative so elaborately layered.

Another phenomenal aspect of the writing are the characters. Every person in TW:EE is special and indispensable for one simple reason; they are all presented realistically, with the flaws and emotions of real people. No one is reduced to solely being a stereotypical fantasy archetype, as everyone has hidden complexities to their backstory, and morally questionable motivations for the things they want; which are always logically justifiable in the proper context. These characters drive the storylines, and motivate the player to care deeply about their decisions.

To top off the narrative adventure, player choice is omnipresent throughout the entire game. There are multiple gut-clinchingly difficult decisions to make about major events, and several reasons to favor any given path. This puts weight behind your choices, as [i]every decision you make could bring devastation; each choice could lead to a greater evil[/i]. The game deftly shows that it understands the importance of consequence, as the epilogue is nothing if not a scathing trial of you as Geralt of Rivia, and the choices you’ve made throughout the duration of your playthrough.

I’ll reveal now that I believe TW:EE may have the best writing of any game I’ve ever played, and [i]I’m not ashamed to say that in the least.[/i]

While I’m admittedly heavily biased due to my obsession with every iota of this franchise, replaying TW:EE has helped me realize that it’s one of my top ten games of all time. Though in some ways a blatant mess, there’s so much narrative expertise and atmospheric charm wholly unique to this game, that I can’t deny being both justifiably, and irrationally in love with it. The Witcher: Enhanced Edition is like your first dog; it’s fussy and a handful because it wasn’t trained right, but you love it unconditionally because of the personal connection you formed with it. The Witcher is an absolute classic, and always will be, in my eyes.

The Witcher was a great playthrough, I'm happy that I chose to experience the first before moving onto the second. I realize I'm late to the party, as the original Witcher came out in 2007, almost 8 years before writing this review. With that said, The Witcher doesn't feel like an out-of-date game. The graphics are still quite beautiful. What I can tell from completing The Witcher is that it had some direct effect on more modern RPGs. 

Witcher brings an adult-theme to gaming. Here you make your choices and face the consequences of those choices. There is no scale of right or wrong. [b]You[/b] are the scale of right or wrong. Your past decisions and the occasional sprinkling of regret are what shape your future actions throughout the story. 

The Witcher has very little hand holding for quests and objectives. It's actually required that you pay attention, follow the dialogue, and consider priorities. The story is driven by interaction, not cutscenes. It truly is a breath of fresh air for someone who wants to be immersed in another world. This requires the player to have that interest: you can't mindlessly  blunder your way to the ending. 

As for the gameplay... If there is anything that should be overstated, it's that you should take your time. I spent 30+ hours in the Witcher, on the hardest difficulty, and I still feel like I don't understand many of the concepts. There are a multitude of customization options to alter your experience. This partially causes some awkwardness with the combat system, particularly with combat controls. I personally played Over-The-Shoulder(OTS) because I felt much more directly involved with the world than either isometric camera. 

The hardest difficulty makes preparation necessary, which definitely adds a dimension to the combat. Knowing how to approach your enemies, researching your foe, utilizing your potions and the proper technique is half the battle. If you've developed your signs or bombs, this adds another dimension. Without that extra difficulty the combat is pretty simplistic, revolving primarily around appropriate clicking for attack combos. There is awkwardness from the controls; even during the epilogue I found myself swapping weapons or signs improperly. It caused some rather obnoxious deaths.

The inventory management is spectacular, simple, effective, easily one of the best I've had the pleasure of using. The same can be said for the crafting/alchemy panels. The journal and glossary are perfectly organized and easily accessible. They provide useful information including direction, extra lore, character knowledge, pictures, and even combat tactics. Character development (leveling up) has a plethora of options which allow for customization based on playstyle. I personally disliked that I couldn't keep Geralt well-rounded, but I can see how this adds replay value. 

The plot is hunt down the bad guy and do some Witcher work on the side. Despite my intention to remain neutral in the ever growing conflict, I eventually chose a side. The side quests were my favorite aspect and where I spent the majority of my time. I had two obvious options for pursuing romances, but neither appealed to me. A perfect example of something becoming greater than the sum of its parts. [quote]The game that kicked things off for an all but unknown franchise. The graphics and voice acting can be ropey, and sometimes gameplay feels repetitive, but for those wanting to immerse themselves in the world of the Witcher and work through the series, there’s no better place to start. Recommended with caveats.[/quote]

It must be stressed that despite looking like a typical third person adventure slash RPG, it isn’t one and is dissimilar to games that it might be initially compared to. Unlike Skyrim or even the later Witcher games this one is in the cRPG mould, with isometric camera options nestled next to the third person that you’re sure to have seen. Quests are plot heavy, with waypoints, and much of the game is set out in notes, letters and journal entries which are critical to fleshing out the plot. It’s for that reason that despite the inevitable search for gamepad mods, the fact that the game is essentially mouse/keyboard controlled is not a problem at all. The game has been engineered with this is mind and it doesn’t diminish the experience at all, with Geralt’s movement, combat and interaction with his environment all coming easily after that initial control acclimation period. It may seem daunting to control Geralt initially, but it quickly becomes second nature.

The Witcher is by no means a bad looking game, but of course it’s become dated and suffers from rubbery looking characters and low resolution textures. By no means are the visuals bad though, and despite there being a plethora of texture and graphic mods available I found the vanilla experience satisfactory…it’s old but not by no means eye wateringly so. The world is lovingly crafted and is realised effectively, transporting the open minded player to Geralt’s world remarkably well, and combined with the wonderful atmospheric soundtrack, whilst character models may be a little ugly, the environments are more than acceptable. The music, albeit standard fantasy fare, is never tiresome although some of the voice acting in the game ranges in quality, again something that is indicative of the game’s age and budget.

Combat is something else that stands out in this game, as some might wonder how Geralt can efficiently cut down his opposition with the keyboard and mouse set up. In fact altercations are handled very simply, with Geralt slipping in to combat mode, drawing his sword of choice (Steel for humans and animals, Silver for the supernatural) and squaring up to his enemies. Geralt has three styles (Strong/Fast/Group) which are very much in the rock paper scissors style – facing a slow but sturdy foe? Cut him down with strong overhead blows, but the same can’t be said if the opposition is more nimble or the enemy outnumbers Geralt three to one. It’s very much the right tool for the right job. Combat itself is essentially rhythm action based with the mouse pointer lighting up to indicate the appropriate time to strike. Time it right and Geralt will be able to string a sequence of attacks together interrupting his opponents momentum, fail and Geralt will be left open to the consequences. It’s a simple system but it works fine. 

Geralt also has access to an arsenal of alchemical potions and magical signs, bolstering his options for survivability and exploration. Knock down enemies with a blast of magical might and kill them outright, or soften them up with a burst of flame or even temporarily disable them. There are five different spell types, each of which offering differing capability, although some are far more useful than others. If Geralt collects ingredients he can also mix potions to aid him on his journey, giving him boosted health regeneration, enhanced reflexes or even night vision (I’d also highly recommend the better colour coding for alchemy ingredients mod to make the process less arduous). It’s a nice addition to the gameplay that whilst a curio on the lower difficulties becomes vital as the challenge is increased. Geralt’s abilities can also be boosted, with the experience system allowing him to allocate skill points as the player progresses through the game. There are myriad options for customisation, and it’s quite difficult to accidentally allocate experience in such a way that will cause undue complications.

However, the biggest stumbling point to player engagement is the gameplay - objectives in The Witcher seem to be very “fetch questy”. Geralt will, more often than not have to go from person one to person two have a chat and perhaps exchange an item, and then return to person one or travel to someone else. All in all, it’s a very dialogue and interaction heavy system of questing and experience and sometimes the sheer amount of walking involved felt tiresome. There’s certainly combat, but sometimes it’d be nice to be “doing” more and being more directly engaged by the game’s mechanics. And because of this even a player insistent on the vanilla experience will want to research the movement speed mods for a much less onerous time.

Taking the game as a part of a series that has improved successively, is this an experience worth having? Experiencing the world, and learning about characters and lore made it worthwhile, and going into the subsequent games it’s a nice foundation to have. As a standalone experience it’s an easy skip, but for the curious player who can accept the age of what’s on offer here I’d cautiously give this a thumbs up.

I came very late to the Witcher series, and decided to start at the beginning - and I'm very glad I did. Though the original Witcher suffers from a few problems as a result of some strange design choices and its age, it is, arguably, one of the best games I've ever played - and certainly better than the game that followed in the series.

Sadly, its first four hours are the worst. The entirely brown landscape of the castle you're introduced to and the initially incomprehensible combat system left me thinking that I should probably just have started at TW2, like everyone said.

If you can stick it out though, there's a moment in the second location you're taken to where everything just... clicks. Suddenly, the way the quests are structured makes sense. The combat system actually becomes quite enjoyable, and the game finally finds its voice.

After that moment, The Witcher suddenly becomes impossible to stop playing. The story ramps itself up to an addictively inriguing level, and the whole atmosphere of the game changes and deepens. Indeed, I don't think that any other game has quite managed to create the 'feel' that the first Witcher has in abundance.

There are a few standout moments of storytelling - and one that totally suckerpunched me, and that I still think about months later - but if nothing else, its the characters that you should stick it out for. A lot of what happens in this first game is very important for what comes later on, and I can't imagine going on to TW2 and 3 without having played this first. Even basic elements of the later stories are informed by the first game.

For its very low price and long playing time, it's an absolute bargain. 

So - if you've come here wondering whether you should start at the beginning, my advice is: do it. I can't recommend it enough.

The Witcher is a strange beast.  At this point, everyone knows how beloved The Witcher III instantly became, and everyone knows it as a true force to be reckoned with in terms of Western RPGs.  So, to preface, the most important thing about getting into The Witcher 1 is to remind yourself that this is not The Witcher III.  Not at all.  The Witcher is clunky, aged, and features some questionable design choices.  But at the same time, it features some great dialogue, story, and setpieces.

Gameplay
--
The hardest part about getting through The Witcher is, regrettably, actually playing it.  The combat is a very simple click in rhythm style affair with two swords for different enemy types and three fighting styles for each sword.  It's not horribly involved, and it's usually more time consuming and frustrating than it is fun.  You are also outfitted with 'signs', an alternative for magic.  These signs vary in usefulness, and I personally didn't use them a lot, with the exception of Igni.  However, I may be underselling them, and they may very well be overpowered.  I'm not sure.  Along with this, the game also emphasizes the creation and consumption of potions, which the game will be nearly unbeatable without.  As your own personal skill does little to influence the battles of this game, potions will be mandatory as a crutch.  The leveling system is also unique, in that every level you get a handful of skill points to put into various skill trees.  But, these skills are divided into bronze, silver, and gold levels.  It takes many, many levels to get gold skills, and I didn't even see any until the final act.  This may be my own fault for not completing every single side quest in the game, but the pacing does feel off.  To level up, create potions, or pass the time, you must meditate, which requires a fire.  It works.

I would be remiss if I didn't address one of my biggest problems with the game.  The quest/level design is designed in such a way that you will spent the majority of your  time running from one end of the act area to the other, repeatedly.  This is a problem in almost every act, barring IV and V where this is slacked a little.  Act I is designed as a ring shaped road with various buildings and divergent paths from it, and it seems every quest phase will take place on whatever the opposite end of the ring you're at is.  Same thing with acts II and III, which both take place in the exact same location (albeit with new locations added for act III), where you must even go so far as to take a ferry ride to another area just to complete some basic quests.  It's monotonous, and it's easily the most glaring fault of the game.  Rather than true gameplay, it's time filler with no actual value added.  For being a game, the actual gameplay is not exactly exceptional.

Story
--
This is where the game actually begins to shine.  This game forces you to make a lot of morally ambiguous decisions that can radically alter how the story plays out.  Do you, a monster slayer, side with a monster for the sake of doing what's right?  Or do you acknowledge that slaying said beast is your purpose in life, and ignore your personal feelings to do what must be done?  Several decisions of this caliber are thrusted towards you, and I sat staring at my monitor more than once, unable to make a choice.  For the most part, the plot itself is gripping.  It's what kept me playing and convinced me to keep coming back.  I will say that it does hit a point where the story becomes almost stupid, but the side quests and implications of character actions save it from being a complete game killer.  The dialogue is a little weird, but appealing.  Many characters use modern slang and sayings despite the game taking place in an 11th century fantasy setting.  It's a little jarring, but not wholly unpleasant.

Graphics/Sound
--
The graphics are, as one would expect, aged.  There are a lot of reused character models, and a lot of these models are downright corny.  The old woman model is especially eyebrow raising.  Some of the areas in the game are crafted quite well, however, despite the level design mishaps referenced earlier.  The swamps feel appropriately foreboding.  The city is as dingy and unfortuante as you would expect.  Sunlit fields are contrasted with noonwraiths, adding a troubling element of horror to an otherwise beautiful scene.  These areas allow the game to truly breathe.  The sound design is rather hit and miss.  Some of the voice acting is as overbaked as the character models, where other voice acting flourishes.  Geralt himself is exceptionally well voiced, sounding both apathetic to the world and caring at the same time.  It's subtle, but effective.  The music is serviceable, but nothing that will make you run out and buy the soundtrack any time soon.

As a whole, The Witcher is really a developmental step for CD Projekt Red, as one would assume.  It sets up the basis of some general mechanics that will be carried on through future The Witcher titles, but it misses the target a lot as well.  That said, it perfectly sets up the rest of the franchise, and has some great moments that will keep you playing.  I do recommend it, but do be warned that it is not the masterpiece the newer games are.

The Witcher: Enhanced Edition Director's Cut is a story-rich fantasy based action adventure R.P.G. developed by CD PROJEKT RED and published by CD PROJEKT RED, 1C-SoftClub. Witchers are professional monster hunters trained in the way of the sword as well as in the knowledge of anatomy and alchemy among many other things in order to combat supernatural horrors that stalk the lands. You take on the role of Geralt Of Rivia, one of the most famous or infamous of the group, who recently returned to the Witcher fortress of Kaer Mohren only to suffer an unsuspected and terrible attack by a powerful and well organized yet unknown enemy. This force manages to storm the fortress, kill one of your ranks and steal some heavily guarded Witcher secrets before sucessfully making their escape. As he and the other Witchers split up and search for this formidable foe, prepare to follow the trail of Geralt as this mission takes him on a far reaching adventure through the kingdom of Temeria filled with political intrigue, racial tensions, magic, monsters and conspiracies. 

[h1] GAMEPLAY[/h1]

As with any R.P.G. worthy of the title you gain experience points as you complete quests, defeat enemies and finish various tasks. These experience points then accumulate until you level up which will grant you a number of talent points which you can then apply to a variety of useful skills for Geralt. When it comes to fighting, I found the combat in this game rather intriguing and quite different from alot of games that I tend to play in this genre. It's definitely not for everyone as it's a bit clunky and takes some getting used to but it's unique nevertheless. Geralt can choose between three different combat stances... fast, strong and group styles. Each of these combat techniques serves a different purpose but it's up to you to determine how best to apply them in battle. Alchemy also factors in heavily in this title as Witchers are known to brew and imbibe a number of potions and tonics in order to enhance their already significant abilities to combat various monsters that they track down. Throughout the course of this game you will come across an expansive number of ingredients, components and lore to use in your alchemical practices. 

Another fine aspect of this great title is choice. You are given various decisions to make during many encounters over the course of the narrative and they matter as the outcome could have important life and death as well as far reaching consequences for Temeria. Yet another thing that I also truly enjoyed in this game was the dice poker minigame that you play from time to time. It's no Gwent but I really liked playing this alot. Lastly I have to mention how much I also cherised the massive codex in this title which is filled with very interesting information on people, monsters, events and locations. In summary, any fan of fantasy based R.P.G.'s should have this impressive title in their gaming library as the gameplay does not dissapoint, however, it is starting to show it's age but more like a fine wine instead of moldy cheese.
 
[h1] VISUALS[/h1]

I remember playing this game before any of the other Witcher titles had even come out so I found the graphical presentation to be very impressive especially when this game made it's debut years ago and even today it still looks quite good in my opinion. Definitely not on par with the sequels graphically but that's to be expected with newer titles but nevertheless a worthwhile effort for the time. A great color palette, some wonderful textures(better in some places than others) and terrific lighting effects are used throughout the game. As far as problems go, you'll still see alot of character models reused and many are just different in color only so be prepared for that bit of repetitiveness. I also had some issues with the camera angles particularly during fights. Moving on, the N.P.C.'s are animated well for the most part, however you'll notice some stiff movements every now and then. The variety of fantastic locations and detailed environments that you traverse really are wonderful and abundant though. Add to that an excellent soundtrack as well as sound effects and you have a complete presentation. In short, while the title is a bit dated graphically it still manages to provide a terrific visual presentation.
  
[h1] CONCLUSION[/h1]

This game brings back so many memories of me staying up all night whenever I could and playing till I just couldn't stay awake anymore...such a great title. I completely enjoyed The Witcher: Enhanced Edition from the thrilling start to the glorious finish as the story is just really compelling and quite thought provoking because the lines between good and evil quickly become blurred. Just because you look like a man doesn't mean that you can't be the biggest meanest monster there is and vice versa. Replayability is high due to the different amount of choices that you can make during the narrative. As options go, because of the age of the game there are no Steam Achievements to hunt down or Steam Trading Cards to collect. Also there is no D.L.C. available as you get the entire story in this single package. This is one of the few games to come out in recent years where they haven't cut parts off and sold them to you later for more money packaged as "Downloadable Content"...truly the end of an era. In the end, The Witcher: Enhanced Edition Director's Cut has all the makings of a great fantasy title with it's compelling story, thrilling combat and fantastic visuals so this game is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to R.P.G., fantasy and story-rich gamers one and all!

Ok, I like this game.

First, if you play this game, don't expect a AAA experience; you wont find it here, even by 2008 standards. You also find that good voice acting in this game is scarce, but the voice acting is overall passable. Combat will feel wonky when you start playing, but one you get used to it, it will feel pretty good, to the point where you may actually prefer it over Witcher 2's combat (I know I do). Unlike the Witcher 2, this game doesn't feel watered down because consoles; this was a PC only game and this was all CD PROJEKT could muster at the time. The first chapter will feel pretty mediocre (although you wont be there long) until the end of it and the swamps in the second chapter will make you want to stop playing (and you will be there a while and you'll be there several times), but other than that, the game's areas are pretty good. In particular, I liked Chapter 4's areas the most. Game graphics are both good and bad; environments and some character models are well done, while others just straight up look cursed. This game can go for less than £1 on sale, so there is no way that I would say that this game isn't worth it; because it is worth it. It also sets Witcher 2 up well and potentially nets you some slightly better equipment for starting that game, which is useful if you play the Witcher franchise on the hardest difficulties (Hard, Dark, Death March!). You will be able to get pretty awesome power-ups for sword fighting, alchemy & signs as you progress. This is a story-heavy game so, if you like games such as Telltale's The Walking Dead, Life is Strange or The Wolf Among Us, you're ought to enjoy this one too.

If you are like me who got to know Geralt of Rivia, the Witcher, through the countless memes and videos and gifs and the upcoming TV Series and etc, and you've been asking yourself "is that game really that good?", the answer is: [i]holy shit it is.[/i]

You play as a member of the group of professional monster slayer known as Witchers. But not *any* Witcher. You play as the Geralt of Rivia, the famed White Wolf who lifted a curse from Princess Adda but was later given for dead. You wake up being found by old friends, of whom you do not remember...

Do not let the "lost memories" part disappoint you. The Witcher is extremely story rich and focused on character development. Throughout my playthrough I didn't feel like some adventurer killing monsters in a swamp, but as man caught in a battle which was not mine, being forced to choose the lesser evil, whilst trying to remember who he is, who he was, not only for himself, but in the eyes of his old friends as well.

The trailers (and general fanbase) point towards a heartless antihero but playing the game showed me the very opposite. It is rare to see a story in which the order, freedom and neutrality paths all blend so well into each other, in spite of the dramatically different (and bitter) consequences of all of them. The Witcher will present you with choices, and yes, *they matter*, they *weight*. The plot will develop and drag you into it, and you may even foresee the plot twist of the plot twist - or not - but all of the experience will have a taste.

The combat system is rather too simplistic. To perform combos, you click once on an enemy to attack, wait the cursor to give a sign, and then click again. Sigils (a.k.a. Spells) sort of break the monotonicity, but only 1 or 2 are really useful. The Alchemy mechanics were pretty neat, but I on Medium difficulty would seldom need potions. As a side note, speaking as someone who was in a HEMA school for almost a year, it was a delight to recognize that some of the first sword combos were beautifully realistic. All later combos turn into a carnival of fantasy, but that's no showstopper. The leveling system was also rather simple, which is good, to let the story  under the spotlight.

Sadly, no achievements and no Linux port; I played half on Windows and half on Linux with Steam Play (not yet supported). It worked on 4K but my 960M would give me only 10FPS. I got 60~FPS with 1440x900 on Linux through Steam Play, but I had a crash about once every hour; still a pretty decent experience.

The Witcher deserves all of its fame, maybe more. I can only feel sorry for myself (and maybe for *you* also) for never playing this masterpiece before. But if none of these arguments convinced you, let me throw in some more: you get the ladies, you get drunk, you play poker (dice).

Now excuse me, I need to go on a quest to learn how to thumb up a game more than once.

If you have played The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, but haven't played The Witcher 1 yet, you should give it a go, because even though it's a decade old games, it still is a pretty good game. And if you haven't played any Witcher game, you should start from The Witcher 1 and play to The Witcher 3.

After beating the game for the first time in medium dificulty I'm writing this review. I took me around 53 hours doing almost all side quests. 

The Witcher 1 is a RPG game. Sincerely I expected more about the options and decisions I could make in the game. Of course, decisions influence the game, but I believe it would be more interessanting if there were more situations for decision making. But in overall it is a nice game with a very interesting history.

History: Resuming, the game is based on a hunt against an organization that stole secrets from a Kaher Mohen, a place where Witchers live and train. Other conflicts arise when the Witcher starts his pursue, including politics ambitions.

Journal: The witcher has a journal where you can access information about his primary and secondary quests, glossary, formulas used in alchemy, locations, characters, bestiary map etc. I enjoyed a lot how the game help the player describing history and characters. I my case sometimes I forgot some stuff, and accessing the journal help me remember important information. The Bestiary is very helpful because there you have information about monsters.

Mechanics: I used third person view camera, but there are other posibilities as well. Mechanics are based in walking, talking and fighting. 

Combat: I enjoyed the combat style. Basically you have 1 steel sword to fight againt humans and a silver sword to fight nohumans. There are other weapons such as axes and daggers, but I didn't use them in the game. I think swords were more effective. You can forge better weapons with runes and meteorites and use blade coatings that can give you until 40% extra damage. Besides the melee weapons, thge Witcher has the Signs, it is the speels he can cast on enemies and himself.

Monters: The Withcer 1 has a lot of monters with description, short briefing etc. I really appreciated it. Monsters drop itens that you can use in alchemy. Level progression in the game is acceptable. As I did the side quests, from the middle to the end of the game I found very easy to kill them.

Alchemy: that's the magic part of the game. You can read books and scrolls to learn how to make potions, bombs and blade coatings. I suggest to read all the books you can to learn them all. However, during the game I basically used 4 or 5 potions. Alchemy is doing with ingredients you get from plants and corpses. There are a lot of itens you can collect but only 7 basic ingredients to mix you potions and bombs. There are special itens you can get in some specific situations, for example, killing bosses.

Books and scrolls: As all RPG games, the more you talk and read, the more information you get. I recommend reading books for having information about formulas used in alchemy, to learn about history and about monsters.

Loot: You can loot trunks, wardrobes etc anywhere anytime, even inside houses. No one will say anything about it. Just loot always you can.

Making money: Developers made a very interesting form of making money in The Witcher. You can do it with Fist Fight at the Inns trought the chapters of the game and also playing poker with specific NPCs. The other possibility is the dice Poker. Fist fight is very easy, but dice Poker is not so easy at all. I always thought in terms of probability but I lost a lot of money. Sometimes it seems that the computer wants you to loose your money. In some situations I had to save the game and load it again after loosing. Depeding on how advanced you are, you can lose 400+ Orens. In my opinion it is not so easy to make money in this game. Even doing side quests money is not enough to buy expensive  books early in the game. You can sold then by around 20% of the buy price. That is rellay important at the beginning. I beat the game with 10k+. I didn't buy any weapons, I found nice swords and always used blade coatings. 

Inventory: The Witcher surprised me with the small inventory the character can carry. It is more realistic, so you can't carry a lot of itens. There is no weight in the game, just the number of itens are taken into account for you inventory. You can let you itens stored by the Inkeeper at the Inn.

Crashes: The game crashed about 10 times, most of them in chapter 5 and I decided to reduce the resolution. It seemed to solve the problem, but I'm not sure what was the problem. I've never had problems with games even heavier than The Witcher. My suggestion is: save the game every time you remember. There is the autosaving, but I strongly suggest to save the game constantly.

Conclusion: If you like RPG games, I recommend you the buy this game and play it. It will let you some nice experiences and enjoy the world created by Andrzej Sapkowski.

I've yet to finish the game but I made my mind up "already" - The Witcher: Enhanced Edition is a truly interesting, well made and good looking game.
Its story is remarkable, characters are well developed - also the secondary ones - artworks and soundtrack are terrific.

I read many complaints reguarding combat mode, so, this is what I think.

Gameplay wise I'm very satisfied:
albeit there's 3 different combat styles and 2 different swords to choose from every time you face a particular enemy (human, monster, big, small, group of..), it's pretty easy to fight. Geralt attacks with combos and you just need to click once to start one; subsequently it's just a matter of clicking again in sync with Geralt's movements, but that's not hard at all to accomplish because the sword's pointer changes color (becoming orange) and you can also hear the blade "swing" when the time comes to click again for another combo. So you just get less clicking, trying to be more precise and you don't need to smash your mouse's left button to kill someone - I agree that's a bit tricky on the first half-hour in game, but that's really it.

The only problems with games like this one (release date: 2008) is that they're quite old for modern Operating Systems and you'll have to have a bit of patience setting them up. I'm still experiencing some random crash - like when I receive a Windows' notification - but if you remember to save often, then it's not a big deal.

Would I recommend The Witcher? I highly do.

Before I begin, I should mention that the hair physics engine in this game is terrifying. Geralt has been thwacked continuously in the face for the past five minutes of conversation, by a Dwarf's beard. I'm fairly sure that despite being conditioned under vigorous training to remain as an efficiently impassive monster-slayer, no one mentioned being assaulted by 6ft of chin hair. 

This has to do weird things to a person.



Early Review: This is the first game in the Witcher Series. I would recommend going for this Enhanced edition if possible and playing the games in their respective release order.

- Firstly, you should expect a great opening video. Very few have made it to my list of scenes that I can not bring myself to skip, each time I start up the game. 


- The protagonist, Geralt, an emotionally-estranged Witcher, also known as the White Wolf (*shivers*...one of my favourite characters of ALL time) combines a fierce combination of strength and brutality in a character, to a promiscuous, yet apathetic personality - strangely alluring, leaving an unusual twist to the standard freedom-fighter hero, present in many other games of this genre. 


- So far, The Witcher's plot is one of my all-time RPG favourites. I find the depth of story highly immersive and believe many who play will come to care greatly for the characters. Rarely am I hooked from the get-go.

You should expect a heavily story-driven state of play, with linear methods of questing, and a nice amount of Lore is available in game.

Sectioned into chapters, the game allows you to progress through the main story at a pace that I would consider to be acceptable.
Many quests available are of no importance to the main story, though provide another welcome layer of depth. As side-quests, they can be missed, but for purposes of enjoyment, I would recommend completing everything.


- Initially, the controls, primarily directed by your mouse, feel very clunky and the interface is slow and methodical - fairly awkward in short, but you will overcome this with ease after a few hours of play. As an Action RPG featuring a hack and slash combat style, I can imagine that this received quite a bit of negative criticism, though personally, I find it rather refreshing from the standard 'mashing your mouse to death' style.

Certain aspects of the game require a little bit of thought - forward planning - which proves the Active-Pause to be quite useful, especially during the rougher combat situations, if you choose to play Hard Mode. 
Playing with the medium difficulty setting, I still found myself challenged to the point that I had to replay certain scenes due to a gory death.

Decision making is also a prominent feature, allowing you to tailor the actions of your protagonist, and the outcomes of your quests.



- Graphically the game is outdated but still looks good by today's standards when used on highest settings.


Highly recommended, a must play for all fans of the RPG genre. 10/10

The Witcher: Enhanced Edition is a bit dated, but still worth playing.

I've had friends recommend I play The Witcher 3, but preferred to start from the beginning - particularly since save files are importable. (And it turns out the default Witcher 2 settings kill off two characters from the first game that are pretty compelling).

This is a game that is clearly designed to be played with a mouse and/or keyboard. Despite this, it has controller compatibility, and I was able to play with a PS4 controller with minimal issues. Still, things often felt a bit janky, and I had to mod the game to increase font size so that I could read the text on my TV screen from my couch. It's a suboptimal control scheme to be sure, but at the end of the day it worked well enough.

This game is before The Witcher went open world, and has a feel like BioWare games from that era (which is unsurprising given the choice of engine). Quests are somewhat open-ended and non-linear within chapters, but the chapter format neatly cabins most content within the confines of a single chapter, creating a very linear experience at the macro level.

The consensus seems to be that "Hard" is the best difficulty to choose, and I agree with that. It makes alchemy relevant to the game, and the long-acting potions and toxicity meters that limit how many you can down at a time are well thought-out. The swordplay is a satisfying rhythm game and not too hard to get the hang of. One frustrating aspect, though, is getting thrown into battle mode and being unable to interact with the environment to gather ingredients or harvest remains. There were many times navigating the game felt like a slog, especially returning to areas you'd already killed plenty of enemies in.

The game places an emphasis on the choices you make, and for the time it was made, it does offer a good amount of branching outcomes for various quests. You're not going to go down starkly divergent paths in terms of base game content (and some decisions frustratingly all lead to the same outcomes with a slightly different flavor of dialogue), but you can clearly see the impact of you choices reflected as you play. These choices play out in a world that is fundamentally grey; sometimes you'll be faced with choices where you have an option that is more clearly "good", but more often than not you're simply left making the best choice you can with the information you have available, and hoping for the best. Often, there is no good choice, and even choices that seem good at the time have negative downstream effects. It can be frustrating in the moment to have to pick from two bad options, but it ultimately serves to make the experience more interesting and compelling.

Though the subject matter is often dark and serious, the game is no stranger to lighthearted and humorous moments. One of the most amazing dialogue trees I've ever had the pleasure of navigating had me debating the finer points of an in-game academic treatise on various alchemical substances with an NPC. Moments like this peppered throughout the game prevent the atmosphere from becoming too oppressive.

It's worth noting that the implementation of "Romance Cards" in this game is somewhat problematic. There are a couple dozen women over the course of the game that Geralt can rendezvous with. Some of these encounters, in and of themselves, are fine. But the game creates a "gotta catch'em all" incentive by providing you with a salacious "Romance Card" for each encounter (though a few double as nightmare fuel). This is a concept that probably wasn't a good idea even in 2007, and certainly hasn't aged well since then. To make matters worse, some of these encounters are, to say the least, uncomfortable. Think a villager who will sleep with Geralt if he gives her some daisies (which he can conveniently find on her fiance's corpse down the road), or Geralt offering some bread to a starving elf, only to have a baffling dialogue exchange that somehow results in a sexual encounter (it was honestly one of the most WTF moments I've ever had in a game).

Despite the dated, janky, and problematic aspects of this game, it's well worth playing even today - at least once. The game does offer replay value by offering three basic branching faction paths. But the core of the game doesn't drastically differ, at least not sufficiently to draw attention away from countless other fictional worlds to explore. At the end of the path I chose, I found myself satisfied with the experience, but not eager to slog through the game's more repetitive moments again to see the variations on the core story line (something I am willing to do with some games). I'll be moving on with the series, with fond memories of this game - but I doubt I'll ever go back to it again.

Hello everyone, you may call me Sapphire. I just finished an attempted 100% run (I missed some things sadly), but I did see most of what this game has to offer, so I thought I should make a review of it. This is my first ever review, so please go easy on me if I miss anything!

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[h2] Quick and dirty version[/h2]

[b]The gist:[/b] this game is old, combat is janky though well defined, the visuals are nowhere close to what you'd expect from a modern game (Although you shouldn't expect that of a game from 20 years ago but since some people only care for visuals I though I'd mention it) and the quality of life isn't exactly there yet, honestly I'd say more than 35% of your play time will be walking from point A to point B, this is the kind of game I'd tell you to avoid if the world and characters and writing weren't so enthralling and good, you will not regret playing this game  if you're a fan of the book or the third game or want to get into the series or if you just want a good dark fantasy story, the big caveat is that the game is quite janky and outdated in many regards which is something a lot of you aren't accustomed to, I'd say give it a try all the same and refund it if you can't help it.

[b]Performance:[/b] I have a modern rig, so I was quite surprised to see this old game run perfectly fine on it. The only problem I ran into was character hair running all wild and shaking during cutscenes, it was annoying, but limiting the game to 60 fps in the Nvidia control made that go away, and I think this game runs pretty smoothly and looks pretty good in 60 fps.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[h2] Long and detailed version[/h2]

[h3]The Positives[/h3]

[b] The Story:[/b] This game's story is stellar, and the world and setting are amazing. There's almost not a dull moment in exploring what it has to offer. I will refrain from spoiling anything, but you will genuinely love every moment here even the slower parts, like chapters one and four which have plenty of intrigue and mystery to go around. I adored almost every moment and character here, especially chapter 2, I think chapter 2 is the best part of this game.

[b]Quest design and writing:[/b] This relates mainly to the side quests of this game, but my golly, are they good! Almost all side quests here have an interesting twist or conclusion, they're full of awesome characters, and a lot of them tie into the main quest, especially in chapter 2, I think most of the quests in chapter 2 tie into the main quest and are interconnected with one another.

[b]Geralt:[/b] A lot of games have silent protagonists or voiced protagonists that are so completely passive they might as well be silent. Geralt is a very good main character and makes me feel like I'm following a seasoned veteran on his journey from the first chapter. The VA and dialogue writers really outdid themselves with him.

[b]Visuals and artstyle:[/b] Yes it's very outdated. Yes, I love outdated graphics! It's a window into the past that I adore. Old games feel so otherworldly in a sense, and if you feel the same way, then you are going to adore the visuals of this game.

[b]Codex: [/b] A weird thing to gush about, but I really enjoyed reading about the world. I think the devs really cared about presenting this setting to non-book readers.

[b] Dice Poker: [/b] I love side activities in games, and I love them even more when they're balanced. Much as I adore Yakuza, some of the minigame completion goals are completely brutal, not dice poker though, you'll have to reload like 5 times to become the dice poker world champion.

[b] A certain blonde:[/b] I won't spoil a thing here, but this game does something very interesting where it doesn't only give you moral choices to weigh on and make but also puts on the social pressure that comes with them, as if you are making a real decision and risking your social standing with people you care about irl.

[h3]The Neutrals[/h3]

[b]Combat:[/b] Combat is fun but not very interesting, it's kind of addictive but you'll grow sick of it when you get assaulted by drowner number 2392938927389 when you're trying to finish a quest.

[b]Alchemy system:[/b] a lot of people really like the alchemy system, and while I do like it on paper, the inventory system makes it a chore.

[b]Certain enemy spam:[/b] if I never see another drowner, it'll be too soon, but I also probably fought, like 5 devourers? maybe less.

[b]Guide:[/b] This game is best played with a guide imo, just to save your time walking around and looking for things, a lot of people wouldn't like this, but the game doesn't convey information that well.

[b]Unexplained intro:[/b] So the intro to this game takes place after the ending of the book, but they keep what happened really vague, I assume to not spoil the books unless I somehow missed a piece of dialogue! If so, pretend this point isn't here, but it was really confusing.

[h3]The Negatives[/h3]

[b]The inventory system:[/b] oof, this is probably the worst thing about this game. It's so tedious and limited, and it makes crafting hell. You have to enter your potions menu to check the recipe, then enter the innkeeper dialogue menu to access your items box since your crafting inventory slots are so limited you almost always need something from your inventory box, then you need to enter the dialogue again just to rent a room, and finally you can access your crafting menu. You have to do this every time you want to craft, "But you can use camp-fires without renting a room." Great, now you have to leave the inn, which adds another loading screen to this combo. What were they thinking? 

[b]Too much walking and fodder enemies:[/b] there's a lot of walking in this game, with a limited fast travel system that's only around in chapters 2 and 3, and along that walking there are tonnes and tonnes and tonnes of fodder enemies that pose no threat and aren't interesting to fight, just there to waste your time.

[b]Chapter 5:[/b] the last two problems are ten times worse in chapter 5, not only do you completely lose access to your item box, thus you can't finish certain quests if you didn't know about this in advance, but also crafting becomes even a worse hell, and this chapter in particular has 5 witcherellion enemies at every corner. At some point I got sick of fighting drowners and bludgeoners (forgot how to spell their names lel) and completely ditched my "100%" to beeline to the end. I genuinely do not know what they were thinking.

[b] Rare but annoying interactions:[/b] very rare, but it's still there. For example, there's a certain quest where someone wants you to kill a group of women. The women offer you sex to spare them and there's no way to spare them without the sex. That kind of felt weird as hell when earlier in the game almost the exact same thing happened, except you could show mercy and compassion but also reject the offer. Also, "The Source" is probably one of the worst quests I had the displeasure of completing.

[b]No Kiryu:[/b] This game does not feature Kiryu Kazuma from the hit series "Like A Dragon" :c

I just got around to finally playing the first Witcher game. If you enjoy story-driven games, where you have non-generic choices and they actually have a meaningful impact on the story, this game is for you.

The Witcher offers a very morally grey world for you to explore that is rich with deep story elements. I was so impressed by the story and characters in this game, that I was even compelled to start reading the books, from which the game is derived, so that I could learn more about the lore and personalities that make up the game.

While I do highly recommend this game, I will disclose that it does have it's share of flaws. The graphics are rather outdated, as it is an older game and, while it does have come with a rather unique and interesting character development system, the actual combat is pretty repetative and uninteresting, especially later in the game, which I have a lot respect for.

In addition to these more upfront issues, the layout of the game can also be listed as a minor issue. There are several quests that will have you running all the way to the other side of the map, just to pick up an item from an NPC, before running all the way back to the other side to drop it off...and then back to the original giver to collect your reward. In short: There is a lot of mindless running. 

Every new area also comes with a number of grind quests, where you will need to kill a number of monsters and collect various parts to turn in for your reward. These quests offer nothing to the story and the rewards are usually just some extra EXP and money (which you get an abundance of through the story quests).

All-in-all, the game's main selling point is the incredible story that it tells and the multitude of ways that you can change and influence that story. I would definately recommend this game for at least one play through, if you can get past the repetative combat and long stretches of running. I would suggest, if you are playing just to experience the story, that you skip over all of the monster slayer quests, as the reward is not worth the initial investment. Another perk of playing this game, is that many of you can import your saved file into The Witcher 2 and many of your choices carry over (for example: certain groups in The Witcher 2 will be friendly or hostile to you, based on your choices in the first game...or you might have a character give you a special gift, for helping them with a problem in the first game).

As an added bonus, the developers were also very true-to-form with the books. The opening cinematic is almost a visual play-by-play of the first short-story with very little creative liberties taken for the sake of marketing or some other business model scheme.


Pros

Incredible story and lore
Morally grey choices that strike out from the generic "good vs. evil" route
Unique character development system
Many cross-over elements that carry into the second game

Cons

Dated graphics
Repetative Combat
Very spread out quest objectives, resulting in lots of running
Unnecessary grind quests
